newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Paris stocks recover despite French left win.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Paris stocks recover despite French left win.

text.p: The Paris bourse clawed back most of its early losses of more than three percent on Monday as investors betted that the new socialist-led government would not adopt radically market-unfriendly policies.
But in currency markets, the dollar climbed to four-week peaks against the mark at the upset left-wing victory in the French parliamentary elections sent players swarming into safe-haven currencies.
Elsewhere in Europe, Frankfurt stocks were not affected by the French gloom, climbing 1.7 percent by midday but London fell on profit-taking in a volatile financial sector.
But most eyes were on the French markets where investors initially took fright at the left's victory which left the Socialists relying on the Communists to form a government.

The blue-chip CAC-40 index plummeted 85.19 points to 2,498.75 within minutes of the opening as markets digested a "worst case scenario" for French markets in which the Socialist-led left would need the Communist Party to secure its parliamentary majority.

But the market recovered its nerve and was only 0.3 percent down by midday. Sectors, particularly dollar-earners, outperformed though others, stocks involved in privatisations and restructurings, suffered. Volume was heavy.

"People aren't that scared," one trader said. "They can't raise taxes. The right already did that. They can make life miserable for companies trying to restructure but they can't stop that. They'll do symbolic things."
The bourse was expected to stay volatile ahead of an announcement by the new government on its policy direction and on the composition.

The big drop in Paris followed a 6.48 percent loss last week in the run-up to Sunday's poll. "One hundred points is a lot after last week's drop," one trader said. "Especially since last week's drop was made with the knowledge that the left would probably win."
Conglomerate Lagardere, down 7.6 percent, and defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, down 6.9 percent, were the top CAC losers as privatisation stocks were the hardest hit in early trade.

In Frankfurt, shares were up 1.6 percent by midday, shaking off worries about the future of currency union. The mini-rally was fuelled partly by the stronger dollar, which improved prospects for exports.
In London by contrast, shares were down 0.5 percent, tracking a volatile bank sector in the wake of the former mutual Halifax Plc market debut as a bank.
The newly floated shares, which began trading at 774-1/2p, saw bank shares initially race ahead, only to crack on profit-taking within the first 30 minutes of the trading session.
"The market was met by a successful Halifax debut, which helped us at the open. But people pulled back, took profits in the banks, and paused to re-assess," said one senior dealer.
In currency markets, the dollar was the darling on traders amid renewed uncertainty about the single European currency.

With the French Socialists reliant on the Communists to form a government and pledging a Europe without austerity, analysts said the market was now fretting that this meant either delay or a broad-based, soft euro.
"Neither of those will be palatable to the European bloc -- near-term it seems the dollar is the winner," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International.
The dollar romped to 1.7257 marks up two pfennigs on the levels of seen in late Europe.

Fears of a broad, weak European single currency were fuelled by French Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande, who called for Italy and Spain to be included in EMU and said all stood to benefit if the euro "no longer means austerity".

"The French election results have increased the prospect of a softer euro. That is clearly bad news for the deutschmark, and clearly the dollar has benefited," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International here.
Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister said the EMU project may enter "rougher waters" in months ahead, and said it would become clear in coming weeks whether the euro would be stable.

In London commodity markets, robusta coffee futures tumbled in early trade with benchmark July opening a sharp $270 down at $2,200 per tonne as the market took a sharp reverse from last week's spectacular rally.

The slide followed a steep 12-percent fall in New York on Friday on frantic speculative selling. By 0850 GMT, the London first-month contract fell further by $330 to $2,140. This compares with last week's 20-month-peak of $2,670.
CURRENCIES AT 1200 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.7255 marks and 116.55 yen compared with 1.7075 marks and 116. 37 yen in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1200 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 24.2 points at 4,597.1
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 7.8 points at 2,576.14
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was up 57.78 points at 3605.62.
PRECIOUS METALS Gold was fixed at $344.00 an ounce, compared to Friday's close of $344.65. Silver was at $4.73, down a cent.
